item.title: Mizan BLE: the Till Next Door
item.description: A phone that pays at a till must never pay the till next door. How Mizan BLE picks the nearest host by smoothed signal strength, what a real iPad and iPhone measured, why the first picker flickered at arm's length, and what iOS does not let a Bluetooth payment do.
item.content:encoded:
Mizan BLE: the Till Next Door

A shop has more than one till. When the payer holds out their phone, Mizan BLE has to pick the till in front of them, not the one a metre to the left, and never guess. The only evidence the phone has is how loud each till sounds: the received signal strength, RSSI, in dBm.

The picker

The phone scans for the Mizan service with duplicates allowed, so each host keeps reporting a fresh reading rather than appearing once. A reading of 127 means "not available" and is dropped. Each host's readings are smoothed with an exponential moving average, ema = α·rssi + (1 − α)·ema, with α at 0.3. A host not heard for two seconds leaves the list.

After at least a second and five readings, the phone offers the strongest host if its average is above a floor, −65 dBm, and leads the runner-up by a margin, 6 dB. Otherwise it says "Hold your phone closer to the till" and keeps scanning.

The picker is a pure type. It takes timestamped readings and a clock and answers with a host, "keep scanning" or nothing, so its tests cover one host, two close ones, a host that fades out and the 127 reading without a radio.

What the devices measured

On an iPad Pro and an iPhone 15 Pro, the smoothed signal read −40 to −55 dBm with the phone beside the iPad, −60 to −66 at arm's length, and −66 to −77 a few steps away. So the −65 floor fell where a payer actually stands. That part of the guess was right.

The rest was not. With the phone held still, the average moved 5 to 13 dB within a second. At arm's length, the screen flipped between the host and "hold closer" two to eight times a second, because the picker chose a host and dropped it at the same line. Any value of the floor would have had its own arm's length.

Choosing is not holding

The fix was to split the question in two. The picker still says what the signal shows right now. A second component, host choice, decides what to offer over time. Once a host is offered, it is kept while it still leads by the margin and its average stays above a drop line 6 dB under the floor, or dips under that line for less than a second. It is dropped at once for a clear rival or when it fades out.

Choosing at one line and dropping at a lower one is hysteresis, the way a thermostat avoids switching on and off every few seconds. The phone now keeps the host it offered through short dips instead of flickering. The phone also draws the signal as bars and dBm while it scans, so a payer asked to hold closer can see why.

A second iPad was not at hand, so choosing between two real tills waits for the next version; scripted rehearsal lanes cover it meanwhile.

What iOS does not allow

Some limits are not in the app's code at all.

  • A peripheral cannot hang up. As the second post described, the iPad ends a link by removing its service.
  • The iPad never learns the phone's signal. RSSI is something a central reads; the host has no way to tell how near the payer is.
  • Message size is negotiated. A link left at Bluetooth's default 23-byte MTU could not carry the 41-byte amount in one write. Current iPhones and iPads negotiate more, and every sender checks its limit before sending; a message that does not fit fails the transaction rather than being split.
  • Scanning with duplicates works only in the foreground, and iOS may slow it over time even there.
  • No payment can start in the background. Core Bluetooth's background modes can keep a session going that the person started, but they do not offer continuous discovery or a dependable launch when a till comes near. A payment that starts with the phone in a pocket needs another trigger, such as a QR code or an NFC tag that opens the app, with Bluetooth carrying the rest.

Where it stands

Version 0.0.1 is done: payments confirm, fail and decline on a real iPad and iPhone, a host left alone times out, and the logs from every device run hold no amount, key or identifier. The next versions test the limits above: two tills side by side and a payment with no manual step but the payer's confirm, then how close iOS lets a payment come to starting without the app open.

The code, the tests and the rehearsal lanes are at github.com/igor1309/mizan-ble.

item.title: Mizan BLE: Every Way a Transaction Ends
item.description: A payment over Bluetooth has one way to succeed and many ways to stop. How Mizan BLE splits each side into a chain of state machines, why the countdown stops once the amount is sent, and how an iPad ends a link it is not allowed to close.
item.content:encoded:
Mizan BLE: Every Way a Transaction Ends

The first post walked through a payment that goes well: lock, connect, amount, confirm, result. Most of the specifying went into the other paths: the payer walks away, the operator changes their mind, Bluetooth drops halfway. Both screens have to say what happened, and they have to agree.

The endings

The user-level spec of Mizan BLE lists fifteen scenarios. Besides success and failure, a transaction can end because:

  • The payer declines. Both screens say so, and nothing is charged.
  • No one connects in time. The host's countdown runs out; it stops advertising and returns to the keypad.
  • The operator cancels. The host sends a sealed end message, and the phone says the host cancelled.
  • The handshake breaks off. The link drops after the host has the phone's key but before it sends the amount. Both say the handshake failed; the operator can broadcast again.
  • The link drops while the payment is processed. The payer has confirmed, the operator has not picked an outcome. The phone says the result is unknown; the iPad says the payer was not told.
  • Bluetooth is off, or not allowed for the app. No payment starts, and the screen says which.

There are also failures one side sees and the other does not. If the link drops before the host has the phone's key, the host never knew anyone was there: its amount stays on air and its countdown keeps running.

One deadline, and then none

The host's countdown is a deadline for the handshake, not for the payment. Once the amount has been handed to the radio, the countdown stops, and nothing after that times out: the payer reads the amount and the operator picks the outcome in their own time. A confirm is never refused for being slow.

The phone has its own deadline: ten seconds from tapping Start to a secure link, so a host that goes quiet mid-handshake does not leave the payer staring at a spinner.

A link the iPad cannot close

Core Bluetooth gives a central cancelPeripheralConnection. A peripheral has nothing like it: the iPad cannot hang up on a phone. So the host ends a link by removing its service. It first sends whatever is queued, such as the result or the end message, then retires the service, and the phone sees the service go. The other direction is cleaner: the host learns the phone is gone when it unsubscribes from To client.

Each radio reports a dropped link, a vanished service or Bluetooth turned off as the same thing, a lost link, so each flow has one loss to handle rather than three.

A chain of state machines

Each side is a chain of small machines. On the host, amount entry types the amount, host broadcast takes it to a secure link, and host payment takes it to a result. On the client, find chooses the host, connect opens the secure link, review takes the payer's decision, and payment waits for the result. The split falls where the work changes: once the link is secure, the countdown and the signal strength stop mattering.

Each machine is a pure reducer, (State, Event) -> (State, Effect?), and an effect handler that hands each effect to an injected dependency and returns its results as events. The reducer never touches the radio, the clock or CryptoKit, so every ending above is a table of events in and states out, tested with no Bluetooth at all.

The machine that started a transaction, host broadcast or client find, does not end when it hands over. It waits, and when the transaction ends it is told and goes back to its start. That way the code that wires the machines together keeps no state of its own about where to return.

Rehearsing without a radio

The simulator has no Bluetooth, but each ending still needs to be seen on a screen. A rehearsal build of the app swaps the radios for a scripted other side, read from a JSON file, that plays the real protocol, with real keys and sealed messages. Fifteen Maestro lanes drive it through every scenario, check the screens, and read the app's log to confirm that no amount, key or device identifier was ever written to it.

The real devices then only had to confirm what the lanes already showed, and they did: confirm, fail, decline and a host left alone all ended as specified on an iPad and an iPhone.

The last post in this series is about the part that did not go as specified: choosing the nearest till by signal strength.

item.title: Mizan BLE: a Payment Between an iPad and an iPhone over Bluetooth
item.description: Mizan BLE is a proof of concept in which an iPad at the till and a payer's iPhone agree a payment over Bluetooth Low Energy. What it is, which device plays which Bluetooth role, and how the four characteristics of one service carry a whole transaction.
item.content:encoded:
Mizan BLE: a Payment Between an iPad and an iPhone over Bluetooth

Some bank apps let you pay at a till by holding your phone near it: no QR code, no card, no tapping through a list of devices. The phone finds the till on its own, shows the amount, and you confirm. I wanted to know how much of that an ordinary iOS app can do over Bluetooth Low Energy, with no special entitlement and no hardware but an iPad and an iPhone.

Mizan BLE is the result: one app with two modes, built to answer that question. It is a proof of concept, not a payment system. The payment is mocked; no money moves.

Two modes

The host is an iPad at the till. The operator types an amount and locks it, and the iPad starts advertising it with a countdown, 60 seconds by default.

The client is the payer's iPhone. It finds the nearest host, and when the payer taps Start, it connects, shows the amount and asks them to confirm or decline. On a confirm, the operator picks the mock outcome, success or failure, and both screens show it.

Either device can take either role: an iPad launches as host and an iPhone as client, and a switch in the header changes it between payments.

Who is the peripheral

Bluetooth LE has two roles. A peripheral advertises and serves data; a central scans, connects and reads or writes. The till is the natural peripheral: it stays put and announces itself. The phone is the central: it looks around, picks one, and starts the conversation.

So the iPad serves one Mizan service and advertises its UUID with the till's name, MIZAN- and four hex digits. The iPhone scans for that UUID only, so it never sees the headphones and watches nearby.

Four characteristics

The whole transaction runs through four characteristics of that one service:

CharacteristicPropertiesCarries
Sessionreadthe host's public key and a session id
Client keywritethe client's public key
To clientnotifythe amount, the acknowledgement, the result, or an end on cancel
To hostwritethe payer's decision

One payment goes like this:

  1. The operator locks an amount. The host makes a fresh key pair and session id, serves the service and advertises. Its countdown starts.
  2. The payer taps Start. The phone connects, subscribes to To client and reads Session.
  3. The phone writes its own public key to Client key. Both sides now derive the same session key. The host stops advertising, sends the amount, sealed, on To client, and stops its countdown.
  4. The phone opens the amount and shows it. The payer's decision goes back, sealed, on To host, and the host acknowledges it.
  5. On a confirm, the operator picks the outcome; the host sends the result. The phone disconnects, and the host removes the service.

On a real iPad and iPhone, from connecting to the amount on screen takes 1.1 to 1.3 seconds.

Nothing in the clear

Every transaction makes fresh P-256 key pairs on both sides. The two run ECDH and derive a key with HKDF-SHA256, salted with the session id, and every message after that is sealed with AES-GCM. The sealed data is bound to the session id, the message type and a counter per direction, so a message replayed, or carried into another transaction, is refused. The largest message, the amount, is 41 bytes, small enough to cross in one write without fragments. All of it is CryptoKit; there is no third-party crypto.

The key keeps out a listener, not a fake till: any device can advertise as a host. A later version could show the same four digits, derived from the shared key, on both screens for the payer to compare, the way Bluetooth pairing does.

Try it

The code is at github.com/igor1309/mizan-ble, MIT-licensed. The tests run with swift test on a Mac; the app needs a real iPad and iPhone, since the simulator has no Bluetooth. A rehearsal build plays the other side from a settings file, so the simulator can run every payment too.

The next post is about the part that took the most specifying: every way a transaction can end, and the state machines that make each one show up on both screens.

item.title: Agonara: Grading Open Answers with a Model
item.description: Agonara can grade a student's open answer with any model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model grades per criterion, its output is validated before a student sees it, and the work runs as a leased, retried, budgeted job.
item.content:encoded:
Agonara: Grading Open Answers with a Model

A multiple-choice check is easy to grade: the student picked an option, and it is right or wrong. In Agonara that is the Quick Check, and no model is involved.

An open answer — "explain why this works" — is where real understanding shows, and where grading is hard. A model can do it, and do it well, but it can also wander: grade against criteria nobody wrote, return a paragraph instead of a verdict, or leak details of the system it runs in. This post is about how Agonara lets a model grade without letting it do any of that.

The curator writes the criteria

An open-answer check comes with assessment criteria, accepted by a curator like any other program content. The model never decides what a good answer is. It gets the student's answer, the exact revision of the check and the exact revisions of its criteria, and is asked one thing: for each criterion, was it met?

The answer has a fixed shape. For every criterion there must be exactly one item, naming that criterion's revision, with an outcome of met, partially met, missing or unclear, and a line of feedback. There is also a short summary.

Check the output, then show it

The request asks for JSON matching a schema, but a schema in the request is a hope, not a guarantee. So the result is checked again when it comes back:

  • exactly one feedback item per required criterion, no extras, no duplicates;
  • every outcome one of the four allowed values;
  • every piece of text non-empty, and free of anything that looks like an operational detail — sessions, cookies, authorization, raw prompts, stack traces, temporary paths, connection strings.

Output that fails is not shown to the student. The attempt is evaluated again, or marked as failed. The raw prompt and the raw model response are not kept; what is stored is the validated feedback and the token usage.

A job, not a request

Grading is not done while the student waits on the HTTP request. Submitting an answer creates an evaluator job, and a worker picks it up:

  • the worker takes a lease on the job, for five minutes, so two workers never grade the same answer;
  • a failed attempt is retried once, a minute later, then marked as failed;
  • each job has a budget: one model call, at most 4,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens.

An attempt is always in a named state — submitted, evaluating, evaluated or evaluation failed — so a stuck model shows up as a failure, not a spinner that never ends.

Any model with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint

The evaluator talks to /v1/chat/completions, with a base URL, an API key and a model name set as environment variables. That covers hosted providers and local servers alike. Without them, everything else in Agonara works; open answers simply wait.

What it adds up to

None of these pieces is clever by itself. Together they let a model take on the slow part of teaching — reading an answer and saying what is missing — while what counts as correct stays with a person, and a misbehaving model costs a retry rather than a confused student.

That closes the series on Agonara. The code, with every module described here, is at github.com/igor1309/agonara.

item.title: Agonara: Drafts Are Not the Program
item.description: In Agonara, model suggestions and curator drafts never become program content by themselves, accepted content is kept as revisions, and a student's answers are pinned to the revision they answered. How the modules keep their own data apart.
item.content:encoded:
Agonara: Drafts Are Not the Program

A learning program changes all the time. A curator rewrites an explanation, splits a concept in two, replaces a check that turned out to be ambiguous. Meanwhile students are reading it and answering it. And with an agent in the loop, there is a steady stream of suggestions that may or may not be any good.

The previous post introduced Agonara. This one is about how it keeps all of that from turning into one tangled table.

Three stages for every piece of content

Content moves through three places, each owned by a different module:

  1. A suggestion. A model, asked by a curator, proposes a draft topic, material or check. Suggestions live in the Curator Workspace and can be listed, read, accepted or rejected there.
  2. A candidate. Accepting a suggestion does not publish it. It turns the suggestion into a draft candidate — the same kind of draft a curator writes by hand. The candidate still has to be reviewed.
  3. An accepted revision. When a curator accepts a candidate, the Corpus records a new revision of that topic, concept, material or check: its title and body, its sources, the rationale, who accepted it and when.

So a model's output is two deliberate steps away from a student. Each step checks that the person is a curator of that program, and each acceptance, or refusal, is written to the audit trail.

Revisions, not overwrites

When a curator edits accepted content, the Corpus does not change it in place. It adds a revision and moves the entity's "current" pointer to it. Earlier revisions stay.

That matters most for students. A student's attempt records the exact revision of the check they answered, and an evaluation is made against the exact revisions of the criteria. If the curator later rewrites the check, the student's old answer still points at the question they actually saw. Their answers, attempts and progress belong to the Student Workspace, and a change to the program never edits them.

Ask, don't read

Who takes part in a program — curators, students, invitations, recovery — is decided by Program Membership. Other modules do not read its tables to find out. They ask it: "is this identity an effective curator of this program?" The rules for invitations and lapsed access live in one place, and changing them does not ripple through the curator and student code.

The same goes for the Admin. Admin is an operational role for the instance: identities, credentials, the audit trail. It does not own program content, and being an Admin does not make you a curator.

One file

All of this sits in a single SQLite file. Every module takes part in backup and restore, so a backup is the whole instance — accepted content and its history, drafts, memberships and every student's work — not a set of exports that may or may not agree.

For a system with one operator, that is the right size: no database server to run, and a backup is one file.

The last post in this series is about the part that needs the most care: letting a model grade a student's answer.

item.title: Agonara: a Learning Program Your Own Agent Can Work On
item.description: Agonara is a bring-your-own-agent environment for learning programs. A curator builds a program from sources, students follow it and prove they understand, and the agent you already use does the drafting, quizzing and grading. What it is and why only a person accepts content.
item.content:encoded:
Agonara: a Learning Program Your Own Agent Can Work On

Learning something serious on your own usually looks like this: forty open tabs, a folder of PDFs, a few long chats with a model, and no clear sense of what you actually know. The material is there. What is missing is the structure: what to study in what order, how to check yourself, and where you are still weak.

AI agents are good at producing that structure — summaries, quizzes, feedback on an answer. They are also good at producing confident nonsense. Agonara is my attempt to get the first without the second. The code is at github.com/igor1309/agonara.

Two roles and a program

Everything in Agonara happens inside a program: a structured course built from sources.

  • A Program Curator builds it: topics, concepts, the materials that explain them, and the checks that test them. The curator also sees coverage gaps — concepts with no material, or no check that tests them.
  • A Student joins a program, reads its accepted material, answers checks and sees where they are weak.

A program can be joined by invitation, and someone who lost access can be let back in. An Admin runs the instance itself — identities, roles, the audit trail — but has no say over program content.

Bring your own agent

Agonara does not ship its own assistant. Curators and students point the agent they already use — Claude Code, Codex or any other — at their Agonara instance, through a set of agent skills and a documented HTTP API.

For a curator, the agent reads sources and drafts topics, concepts, materials and checks. For a student, it can quiz them and help them through the material. The web screens and the agents talk to the same API, so what an agent drafts lands in the same place a curator reviews it in the browser.

Using the agent you already have also means you pay for one subscription, not two, and keep the model you trust.

Only a person accepts content

This is the one rule that shapes the rest. An agent can draft as much as it likes; nothing it writes reaches students until a curator accepts it. Suggestions and drafts live apart from the accepted program, and accepting one is a deliberate act by a named person, recorded with who and when.

The same holds for grading. Open answers can be evaluated by a model, but the model grades against criteria the curator accepted, and its output is checked before a student sees it. The third post in this series is about that.

Try it

You need Docker:

git clone https://github.com/igor1309/agonara.git
cd agonara
AGONARA_BOOTSTRAP_SECRET=choose-a-secret docker compose up --build

Open http://127.0.0.1:18080/admin, create the first Admin with the bootstrap secret, then go to /learn. Everything runs without a model; grading open answers needs one behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set with three environment variables described in the README.

Status

Agonara runs as a private instance. Identity, membership, curation, reading, open-answer and Quick Check assessment, learner state, readiness checks, coverage gaps and model-assisted curation suggestions are implemented, each with its own screen. The code is public to read; it is not open source.

The next post looks at how Agonara keeps drafts, the accepted program and a student's progress apart.

item.title: Agister: a Code Review With a Debate Inside
item.description: The code review that ships with Agister runs several lenses in parallel, one of them a writer–critic debate in a bounded repeat, before a judge merges the findings. How it is composed from settings.
item.content:encoded:
Agister: a Code Review With a Debate Inside

Asking one model "review this diff" gets you a review. It is usually plausible, partly right, and blind in ways that depend on the model and the prompt. The home folder that ships with Agister contains the review I actually use, and it is built differently: several focused lenses, a debate inside one of them, and a judge at the end. All of it is settings, in home/.

Five lenses

code_review takes a base revision, a candidate and a goal file, and runs five lenses: architecture, tests, adversarial, clarity and intent — does the change do what its goal says. Each lens is a process with its own prompt and a narrow question. Each is a step, a process bound to an agent, so each can run on the model and effort that suits it.

The lenses sit in a parallel item. Parallel in Agister can be capped: the shipped review sets max: 1, so the lenses run one at a time and share the machine politely; raise it and they run at once. Either way one failing lens does not stop the others — at least one must complete — and the output is a list of each lens's status and output, in declared order. A review where one lens timed out is still a review, and the record says which lens is missing.

A debate in a bounded repeat

The tests lens is itself a workflow, tests_debate. One model drafts the review. Another critiques it. The writer revises in its own session — it keeps the context of its draft — until the critique converges or two passes have run. Only the last review reaches the judge.

In settings this is a repeat item: a body, a state, a next binding over that state and an until condition, with a max. Conditions in Agister are pure: they read params, inputs, the repeat's state and the outputs of items that already ended, with equals, present, all, any, and, or and not. The repeat never reads until before the first pass, and max guarantees it ends.

Why a debate for tests specifically? Test review is where a single model is most easily satisfied: tests exist, they pass, coverage looks fine. A critic whose only job is to push back catches tests that assert nothing or test the mock.

A judge

The judge is one more step, on a different model. It receives the lenses' outputs, each checked against its process's output schema, and rules only on the evidence they present — it does not go back to the code. It checks each finding's severity against its evidence, merges findings that make the same claim across lenses, sorts them, and rejects those whose evidence does not hold: no concrete case, a claim asserted but not traced, or evidence another lens contradicts. A lens that produced nothing is recorded as a coverage gap, never as an approval.

Schemas make this possible: the judge reads structured findings, not five essays.

Why compose instead of prompt

All of this could be one giant prompt. Splitting it gives three things:

  1. Each part is replaceable. Try a different model for the critic by editing one agent file. Settings layer by field — home, repository, project — so a repository can override one lens without copying the rest.
  2. Each part is visible. The record shows each lens, each debate pass with its state and why the repeat stopped, and the judge's input.
  3. Failures stay small. A lens at capacity is retried, then falls back to its agent's fallback if it names one; the review goes on.

What Agister does not do is decide what the findings mean. The review produces findings; acting on them stays with the caller.

Read how settings are layered and resolved, or browse the review's settings in github.com/igor1309/agister.

item.title: Agister: What a Run Leaves Behind
item.description: Every Agister run leaves a folder with the exact definitions by digest, inputs, permission plan, events and patches. Why the record matters more than the terminal output when agents do the work.
item.content:encoded:
Agister: What a Run Leaves Behind

When an AI agent does a piece of work, the interesting questions come later. Why did the review miss that bug? Which prompt was it — the one before or after I edited it? Which model ran, at what effort, with what permissions? How much did it cost? Was the worktree clean when it started?

A terminal scrollback answers none of these. Agister is designed so that every run answers them from a folder on disk.

The folder

Each run is a folder under ~/.agister/runs, named by its start time in UTC and six random hex characters. Inside:

  • record.json — the request, status and result, and every call that ended: its process, agent, inputs, permission plan, environment, the definition files by digest, the HEAD and content it left, its cost and its result. Child workflows appear under children, each with its params, inputs and output.
  • events.jsonl — one line per event as it happens: a step started or reused, a tool call, a turn that went stale, a turn at capacity, a fallback to another agent, a branch taken with each condition it read, a repeat's pass and why it stopped.
  • definitions/ — the actual bytes of every settings file a call was made from, by digest.
  • patches/ — for calls that pinned a revision, the changes they made.

The record keeps the definitions themselves, not their names. Prompts change daily. A month later, "the code_review workflow" means something different; the digest and the bytes do not.

Names you can grep

Steps have stable names that carry their position in the workflow. A step inside a repeat is named by its pass, fix/2/1; a step inside a child workflow is named under the item, tests/revise/1. The call, its record entry, its progress line, its events and its reuse all use that name. "What did the second pass of the fix loop do?" becomes a search, not an investigation.

Records that pay for themselves

A record is not only for reading. Two flags use it:

  • --reuse <run id> runs a request again but takes an earlier call in place of making it, when its process, agent, inputs, definitions and environment are the same and the worktree is as that call left it. Change one prompt late in a long workflow and only the affected steps run again.
  • --continue <run id> goes on in the session of a one-step run's call.

Reuse is only safe because the record is precise. Without digests of definitions and a fingerprint of the worktree, "same as last time" would be a guess.

What the record does not decide

Agister runs what settings define and records it. Committing, pushing, deciding what a review's findings mean, and asking the owner stay with whoever called it. That boundary is deliberate: the runner is the part that should be boring and exact, and judgement belongs to the caller — a person, or another agent with its own instructions.

Progress goes to stderr as it happens; the result goes to stdout as JSON; agister runs export copies a run out. Everything else is in the folder.

Read the run architecture for the full picture, or the code at github.com/igor1309/agister.

item.title: Agister: Agent Work as Settings, Not Code
item.description: Agister is a Go command-line runner for AI-agent work defined in settings files — agents, processes and workflows — with a record of every run. What it is and why I built it.
item.content:encoded:
Agister: Agent Work as Settings, Not Code

The projects earlier in this series — RexLab and FolioTell — were built with AI coding agents. After a few months of that, the hard part was no longer getting an agent to write code. It was everything around it: which model with which effort for which job, what each call was allowed to touch, how a review was put together from several lenses, and, afterwards, what actually happened in a run that went wrong.

I kept solving these with shell scripts and prompt files, and kept losing track. Agister is the tool that replaced them. The code is at github.com/igor1309/agister.

Three kinds of settings

Agister describes work in three kinds of documents:

  • An agent picks a runtime — Claude Code, Codex or bash — and, for a model, which model and effort.
  • A process says what one call needs: its inputs, its prompt, the shape of its output as a JSON schema, and the permissions it asks for.
  • A workflow composes steps — each a process on an agent — and other workflows: in sequence, in parallel, on a branch, or in a bounded repeat.

That separation is the point. "Review this diff for test quality" is a process. "Use a strong model at high effort" is an agent. "Run five review lenses in parallel, then have a judge merge them" is a workflow. Each can change without touching the others, and nothing about the work lives in Go code. Code adds only a new runtime or a new kind of input source.

Resolve first, then run

Before anything runs, Agister resolves the request into definitions or a refusal. A process that needs a permission its agent's runtime cannot grant is refused. A workflow that references a missing document is refused, with the chain that leads to the fault. agister check resolves every document and refuses exactly what a run would.

That gate matters with agents. A misconfigured run that starts, spends twenty minutes and money, and fails at step four is far worse than one that never starts.

Every call ends the same way

Whatever the runtime, every call ends in one result shape: status, output checked against the process's schema, cost. And every run leaves a record — the exact definitions with their digests, the inputs, the permission plan, the events and the outcome. When something goes wrong, there is something to look at besides a scrolled-away terminal. The second post in this series is about that record.

Try it without a model

The simplest agent is bash: a process's prompt is its script, and each input is an environment variable. The README walks through a "Hello, world" run that needs no model and no API key, and leaves a full record under home/runs/.

Agister also ships a home folder with a multi-lens code review — the workflows I use every day — and an implement process. The third post looks at how that review is composed.

Status

Agister is a working tool I use daily to implement and review code with AI agents. Settings and records are versioned formats (v1alpha1) and may still change. The code is public to read; it is not open source.

Documentation: how a run executes and how settings are read, layered and resolved. Code: github.com/igor1309/agister.

item.title: FolioTell: Where Am I in This Text?
item.description: Skipping by sentence and resuming where you stopped sound trivial. In FolioTell they meant mapping UTF-16 offsets from the speech engine back to sentences in the original text.
item.content:encoded:
FolioTell: Where Am I in This Text?

Two features of FolioTell look like one-liners on a product list: "previous or next sentence" and "remembers where you stopped". Both depend on one question the app has to answer all the time: where in the text is the voice right now?

The engine speaks in UTF-16

AVSpeechSynthesizer reports progress through a delegate callback that says which range of the utterance it is about to speak. That range is an NSRange, which means UTF-16 code units, relative to the utterance, not to the document.

Swift strings, meanwhile, are collections of grapheme clusters. An emoji, a combining accent or a Cyrillic letter with a diacritic can be one Character and several UTF-16 units. Mix the two and positions drift: after a few non-ASCII characters, "resume here" lands mid-word.

FolioTell picks one unit and sticks to it. Every position in the playback state is a UTF-16 offset into the speech text: where the current utterance started, and how far it has been spoken. When a word-boundary callback arrives, the reducer adds the utterance-relative offset to the utterance's start and clamps the result to the text's length. Converting to String.Index happens only at the edges, when Foundation needs one.

Sentences from Foundation, not from regex

"Next sentence" needs a definition of a sentence. A regex on full stops fails quickly: abbreviations, decimals, ellipses, quotes, and Russian punctuation rules all disagree with it.

Instead, PlaybackPositionMapping asks Foundation:

text.enumerateSubstrings(
    in: text.startIndex..<text.endIndex,
    options: [.bySentences, .substringNotRequired]
) { _, sentenceRange, _, stop in ... }

and converts each sentence's start to a UTF-16 offset. From there the rules are simple:

  • Next is the first sentence that starts after the one containing the current offset, or nothing at the end.
  • Previous is the start of the sentence before the one containing the current offset, or the beginning. Like most audio players, a tap goes to the previous sentence, not to the start of the current one.

A jump then restarts the utterance from that offset with a new utterance token, so callbacks from the abandoned utterance are ignored (the previous post explains the token).

Resuming after a relaunch

There is a wrinkle: the voice speaks the speech text — the Markdown after heading, list and emphasis markers are stripped — while the file on disk still has them. An offset in one is not an offset in the other, and the speech text changes whenever the normalization rules or the front matter setting do.

So FolioTell saves its place as an anchor in the original document. When it derives the speech text, it also keeps, for every unit of speech text, the source offset it came from. Saving maps the spoken offset back to the document; reopening maps the anchor forward to the first speech offset at or after it, and then to the start of the sentence containing it. A slightly earlier point is better than starting mid-sentence when you have forgotten the context. The sentence starts are kept sorted, so the lookup on every spoken word is a binary search.

Tested in two languages

The tests for this part are deliberately bilingual: English and Russian sentences, front matter skipped or read, each case pinning an offset and checking the jump or the resume. It is the kind of code where an agent's confident "this should work" means little and a failing test with a Cyrillic sentence means a lot.

item.title: FolioTell: a Speech Synthesizer Behind a Reducer
item.description: AVSpeechSynthesizer is asynchronous and full of late callbacks. How FolioTell keeps playback correct with pure reducers, effect handlers and utterance tokens.
item.content:encoded:
FolioTell: a Speech Synthesizer Behind a Reducer

On the surface a text-to-speech player has a handful of buttons: play, pause, stop, skip, speed. Underneath, AVSpeechSynthesizer is an asynchronous engine that reports back through delegate callbacks — a word is about to be spoken, an utterance finished, an utterance was cancelled — and those callbacks arrive after you already changed your mind.

Tap "next sentence" while a word is being spoken and the synthesizer may still tell you about the old utterance: one more word boundary, then a cancellation. Handle those naively and the player jumps back, stops when it should be speaking, or resumes a word too early. FolioTell treats this as a state machine problem.

Events in, state and effects out

The playback logic lives in FolioTellCore, a library with no UIKit, no SwiftUI and no AVFoundation. Its core is a reducer:

func reduce(_ state: State, _ event: Event) -> (State, Effect?)

Every button tap is an event (primaryTapped, stopTapped, jumpToNextSentenceTapped, speedChanged, …), and so is every synthesizer callback (willSpeakRange, utteranceDidFinish, utteranceDidCancel, pauseResolved, …). The reducer computes the next state and, optionally, an effect: start an utterance, restart it from an offset, pause, deactivate the audio session. An effect handler performs it against the real engine through an injected adapter.

A small runtime, RxViewModel, ties it together on the main actor: events enter one funnel, the reducer runs, effects may dispatch follow-up events, and those are processed in FIFO order. Nothing re-enters the reducer while it is running.

Utterance tokens

The key idea for the late-callback problem is a token. Every time playback starts a new utterance — on play, a jump, a speed or voice change, start over — the reducer increments utteranceToken and stamps the new command with it. Every callback carries the token of the utterance it is about.

The reducer then accepts a callback only when the token matches the current session:

case let .speaking(session) where session.utteranceToken == utteranceToken:

Anything else is stale — a replaced utterance, a stop already applied — and is ignored. Changing speed mid-sentence becomes simple: bump the token, restart from the current offset, and let the old utterance's cancellation fall on the floor.

One subtle case is documented right in the code: a word-boundary callback can land just after an accepted pause. The paused state must still track it, or resume would repeat or skip a word.

Why this shape

Three reasons, in order of importance:

  1. Testability. Every race above is a sequence of events. A test feeds the reducer "play, word at 40, next tapped, word at 52 with the old token, cancel with the old token" and checks the state. No simulator, no timing. Most of the 196 tests look like that.
  2. Working with agents. A reducer gives an agent a narrow, well-tested surface. It can add a feature — say, start over — by adding an event and a case, and the existing tests say whether it broke a race it never thought about.
  3. Replaceable edges. The synthesizer and the position store are adapters. The app wires real ones; tests wire fakes.

Remembering where you stopped is a second reducer with the same shape, PlaybackPosition, so the two concerns never tangle.

item.title: FolioTell: an App That Reads Your Notes Aloud
item.description: FolioTell is an offline iPhone app that reads Markdown and plain-text files aloud. Why it exists, and why it has no account, no backend and no network.
item.content:encoded:
FolioTell: an App That Reads Your Notes Aloud

I write a lot in Markdown: notes, drafts, research summaries, documentation. Much of it I would happily listen to on a walk instead of reading at a desk. Yet every way of doing that was awkward. Screen readers are built for navigation, not for long-form listening. Text-to-speech services want an upload, an account and a subscription. Pasting into a "read this" app loses the file and my place in it.

FolioTell is the small app I wanted: open a .md or .txt file where it already lives, press Play, and listen. The source is at github.com/igor1309/foliotell.

What it does

  • Opens files where they are: On My iPhone, iCloud Drive or any Files provider, through the system document browser. No import, no copy.
  • Reads them on the device with Apple's speech synthesis. The voice follows the document's language — English or Russian — or you choose one.
  • Playback controls: play and pause, previous or next sentence, stop, start over, and speeds from 1x to 2x.
  • Remembers where you stopped in each document.
  • Handles front matter: a YAML header at the top of a Markdown file is skipped, or read aloud if you prefer.
  • Suggests a better voice: when only a standard-quality voice is installed for a language, it tells you where in Settings to download an Enhanced or Premium one.

What it does not do

FolioTell is read-only and offline. There is no account, no backend, no analytics, no subscription and no network access at all.

That list is the product as much as the features are. Notes are personal. A tool that reads them should not need to see them anywhere but on the phone. Apple's on-device voices have become good enough — especially the Enhanced and Premium ones — that the cloud adds little for this job.

Being read-only also keeps the app honest about its scope. It does not try to be an editor or a notes app. Your files stay in whatever app or sync service you already use; FolioTell is just a speaker.

Markdown is not prose

Reading a Markdown file aloud naively is unpleasant: "hash hash Introduction", "asterisk asterisk important asterisk asterisk", "dash dash dash". Before text reaches the synthesizer, FolioTell strips heading markers, list markers, quote markers and inline emphasis, drops delimiter-only lines like ---, and collapses blank lines. Code inside fences is kept as written, because there the characters are the content.

It is a small, pure function with its own tests, and it makes the difference between "a text-to-speech demo" and something you can listen to for half an hour.

How it is built

Swift 6 and SwiftUI on iOS 26: a DocumentGroup app over AVSpeechSynthesizer. The playback logic is a separate library, FolioTellCore, made of pure reducers and effect handlers, with the speech engine and storage behind injected adapters. 196 Swift Testing tests cover it, and Maestro flows drive the playback controls on a simulator. Like the other projects in this series, it was built with AI coding agents working from specs and tests.

The next two posts look inside: the reducer architecture, and the surprisingly tricky problem of knowing where in the text you are.
